samples.text:
The bar chart shows how many minutes children aged 8 to 12 spent on five activities every day in 2004 and 2024, and the pie chart shows which devices they used for going online in 2024.

Overall, children spent much more time online in 2024 and less time on most other activities. Smartphone was the most common device.

In 2004, children watched TV for 125 minutes a day and played outdoor for 115 minutes, and these were the main activities. However, in 2024 these activities fell a lot, to 48 minutes for TV and 52 minutes for outdoor play. In contrast, the time for online and games increased dramatically from 20 minutes to 175 minutes, so it became the most popular activity. Reading also decreased from 35 to 22 minutes, and homework went down a little from 45 to 40 minutes.

About the devices, almost half of children used smartphone (46%) and 31% used tablet. Games consoles was 12% and laptop or PC was 9%. Only 2% of children uses smart TV to go online.
samples.why: Brief overview covering both visuals · key changes identified with accurate figures · basic linking (However, In contrast, About) · some awkward phrasing · frequent article and agreement errors that do not obscure meaning.

samples.text:
The bar chart compares the average time that children aged 8 to 12 in one country spent on five daily activities in 2004 and 2024, while the pie chart shows the main devices they used to access the internet in 2024.

Overall, time spent online or playing games rose dramatically, whereas all the other activities declined, particularly watching TV and playing outdoors. In 2024, smartphones and tablets were the devices children used most for going online.

In 2004, TV and outdoor play dominated children's days, at 125 and 115 minutes respectively, while only 20 minutes were spent online or on games. Twenty years later, this pattern had been reversed. Online activities and games took up 175 minutes per day, almost nine times as much as before, whereas TV viewing fell to 48 minutes and outdoor play to 52 minutes, both less than half their earlier levels. Reading time also dropped from 35 to 22 minutes, but homework changed very little, falling slightly from 45 to 40 minutes.

As for devices, smartphones were the most popular, used by 46% of children, followed by tablets at 31%. Games consoles and laptops or PCs accounted for 12% and 9% respectively, and smart TVs only 2%.
samples.why: Clear overview of the reversal in activities and main devices · key features highlighted with apt multiples · good cohesion · some less common vocabulary (dominated, took up) · one minor structural slip.

samples.text:
The bar chart compares how children aged 8 to 12 in one country divided their time between five daily activities in 2004 and 2024, and the pie chart identifies the main devices they used to go online in 2024.

The most striking change was the explosive growth in time spent online or gaming, which became by far the largest daily activity, while television viewing and outdoor play fell sharply. Handheld devices, particularly smartphones, were the main means of internet access.

In 2004, television and outdoor play were children's principal pastimes, occupying 125 and 115 minutes a day respectively, whereas online activities and games accounted for a mere 20 minutes. By 2024, the latter had soared to 175 minutes, almost three hours, which exceeded the combined time spent on all four other activities (162 minutes). Television and outdoor play had both more than halved, to 48 and 52 minutes, and reading had fallen from 35 to 22 minutes. Homework was the most stable activity, decreasing only marginally from 45 to 40 minutes.

Smartphones were the leading device for going online, used by 46% of children, with tablets second at 31%. Games consoles (12%) and laptops or PCs (9%) were far less common, and smart TVs were negligible at just 2%.
samples.why: Perceptive overview · data selected skilfully with an insightful derived comparison (162 minutes combined) · cohesion smooth throughout · precise vocabulary (pastimes, explosive growth, negligible) · wide range of error-free structures.
